summary.text: 弟 commonly means ‘younger brother’ and also ‘junior.’ Early forms have been interpreted as a binding around an implement, but that picture alone does not explain the sibling meaning. A Western Zhou bronze inscription provides the earliest securely sourced sibling use in this evidence.

formation.text: Pictographic: the proposed picture is a binding wrapped around an implement, variously interpreted as a weapon shaft or peg. The further idea that orderly binding suggested sequence and then sibling rank is an interpretation; no earlier sequence sense is securely dated here.

components.text: 弟 is treated as one picture of a binding around an implement, not as a proven combination of current components. The object is interpreted variously as a shaft or peg; early forms are described with an element identified as 必/柲, while some bronze forms are described with 弋. No sequence among these forms is established.

history.text: Oracle-bone and bronze forms are reported, but a continuous graphic sequence to the modern form is not established. The Shuowen account describes successive leather bindings and says the graph follows an ancient form; this is a historical explanation, not a verified reading of the earliest picture.
In 第, 弟 serves as a phonetic component. This sound role belongs to 第 and does not make 弟 itself a phonosemantic compound.

Japanese word history distinguishes native oto/otōto from the Chinese-derived reading てい. A source cites oto for a younger person of either sex in 712 and describes the narrowing of おとうと to younger male sibling as an Edo-period development. This is Japanese word history, not a meaning development of the Chinese character.

uncertainties.text: The proposed implement’s spoken name is not established, so borrowing the graph for ‘younger brother’ because the words sounded alike remains a possible mechanism, not a demonstrated sound match.

The early forms do not establish an early ‘younger brother’ meaning. A cited Western Zhou bronze inscription uses 弟 in 兄弟, but its exact date is unresolved; an earlier sequence or rank use is not established.

senses.period: Western Zhou bronze inscription evidence; exact date unresolved
senses.text: A cited Western Zhou bronze inscription uses 弟 in 兄弟. This is the earliest securely sourced sibling use here, but it does not show that the earliest oracle-bone forms already had this meaning.

senses.gloss: junior; younger person or lower in rank
senses.text: 弟 is also used for junior status and sequence or rank. When these uses began, and whether one developed from the other, is unresolved.

senses.period: Attestations cited from a Tang poem and later literature; witness dates not checked
senses.text: In literary contexts, 弟 can serve as humble self-reference among peers. Its earliest use and path from a junior designation are unresolved; this sense does not show that the character originally meant ‘I.’
Classical citations are reported for female younger-sibling or junior uses. Their dates and relationship to the broader junior sense are unresolved.

developments.text: Humble self-reference may be pragmatically related to a junior or younger-peer designation, but the pathway and earliest use are unresolved.

limitations.text: The binding-to-sequence account is an interpretation, and no independently dated sequence or rank use earlier than the sibling sense is established. A semantic chain between these senses cannot be specified.
The evidence gives separate readings and senses, including an ethical 悌-related use, but does not establish a unified development connecting them to the common sibling meaning.

overview.text: 弟 commonly means ‘younger brother’ and can also mean ‘junior.’ Its early form is interpreted as a binding around an implement, but the picture alone does not explain the sibling meaning.

components.text: Read 弟 as one proposed picture of a binding around an implement; the object and the picture’s interpretation remain uncertain.

takeaway.text: Sound borrowing may explain the sibling meaning, but the implement’s name and a sound match are not established.
